unit.unitTitle: Multiplying and Dividing Fractions and Decimals
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 15! In this unit you will learn how to multiply and divide unit fractions and how to multiply decimals by whole numbers. These are some of the most useful skills in all of mathematics, because they turn up every single day. When Amina measures out 3/4 of a cup of butter to bake anjero for the family, when Yusuf works out the cost of three shirts at 4.60 each at the Hargeisa market, or when Halima shares half a mango fairly between her little brothers, they are all multiplying and dividing fractions and decimals.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 5 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: This unit is designed for self-paced learning. That means you move at your own speed. Read each explanation slowly, work every example yourself on paper before you look at the solution, and only move on once you feel steady. Your AI tutor is available day and night to give you extra practice, explain a step in a fresh way, or check your working. Your teacher will also meet with you about twice a week to help with anything that feels tricky, so you are never learning alone.

Why does this matter so much? Fractions and decimals are the language of measuring, sharing and money. Traders in the market use decimals to add up prices and give the right change. Cooks use fractions to scale a recipe up for a big Eid gathering or down for one person. Families share food fairly at iftar during Ramadan. Builders and tailors measure in fractions of a metre. When you become confident with these operations, you gain a skill you will use for the rest of your life, and you build the foundation you need for percentages, ratio and algebra in the years to come.

As you work, keep a pencil and paper beside you and always draw the picture. Mathematics is not a subject you can learn only by reading; you must do it. Draw the bar, shade the parts, mark the number line, and say the answer out loud. If you make a mistake, that is not a failure. It is simply a signpost showing you exactly what to practise next. Every mathematician you admire once sat where you sit now, learning these very same ideas one careful step at a time.
Multiply a unit fraction by a whole number, for example 1/5 × 4 = 4/5.
Divide a unit fraction by a whole number, for example 1/4 ÷ 2 = 1/8.
Multiply a decimal number (with tenths) by a whole number, for example 12.9 × 6 = 77.4.
Use bar models and number lines to represent fraction and decimal operations.
Explain the link between repeated addition and multiplication of fractions and decimals.
Estimate an answer before you calculate, and check the answer is reasonable.
Solve real-world word problems and choose the right operation each time.

concepts.title: Fractions and Decimals in Daily Life
concepts.explanation:
Before we learn the methods, let us see why this maths is worth learning. Fractions and decimals are everywhere around you, hiding inside ordinary jobs you do without thinking.

In the kitchen: a recipe says “use 3/4 cup of butter.” If Khadija wants to make two batches for a family gathering, she needs 3/4 × 2 = 6/4 = 1 1/2 cups. Multiplying a fraction told her exactly how much to measure.

At the market: one shirt costs 4.60 shillings. If Omar buys three shirts for his brothers, the total is 4.60 × 3 = 13.80. Multiplying a decimal told him the total cost so he could count out the right money.

Sharing with friends: Hassan has 1/2 of a pizza and wants to share it equally among 4 friends. Each friend gets 1/2 ÷ 4 = 1/8 of the whole pizza. Dividing a fraction told him exactly how much each person receives.
concepts.example: Notice that all three jobs used the same three operations you will master in this unit: multiplying a fraction, multiplying a decimal, and dividing a fraction. The maths is not separate from life; it is life, written in numbers. Keep these three stories in your mind as you learn, because every rule you meet is really a shortcut for a picture like these.

concepts.title: Multiplying a Unit Fraction by a Whole Number
concepts.explanation:
When we multiply a unit fraction by a whole number, we are finding how many of those fraction pieces we have altogether. Think of it as repeated addition, exactly the way multiplying whole numbers is repeated addition.

Look at 1/5 × 4. This means “four pieces of 1/5”, which is the same as:

We can picture this with a bar model. Draw a whole bar and split it into 5 equal parts, because the denominator is 5. Then shade 4 of those parts, because we want four pieces of one fifth. The shaded amount is 4/5.

Whole bar in fifths: [ _ | _ | _ | _ | _ ] → shade four: [ ■ | ■ | ■ | ■ | _ ] = 4/5

We can also picture it on a number line from 0 to 1, split into fifths. Starting at 0, we hop forward 1/5 four times: to 1/5, then 2/5, then 3/5, then 4/5. We land on 4/5, the same answer the bar model gave us.

0 ——1/5——2/5——3/5——4/5——1 (four hops of +1/5)

Let us calculate 1/7 × 3 carefully, one step at a time.

Draw a bar split into 7 equal parts, because the denominator is 7.

Shade 3 parts, because we want three groups of 1/7.

Count the shaded parts: there are 3 parts, each a seventh, so 3/7.

Do you see what happened? The denominator stayed the same (still sevenths) while the numerator grew from 1 to 3. That gives us a quick rule that always works.

⭐ Quick Rule To multiply a unit fraction by a whole number: keep the denominator the same, and multiply the numerator by the whole number. 1/n × a = a/n. For example 1/6 × 5 = 5/6, and 1/9 × 12 = 12/9 = 1 3/9 = 1 1/3.

Sometimes the numerator grows past the denominator, and then the answer is more than one whole. Take 1/4 × 6. Keeping quarters and growing the numerator gives 6/4. Because 6 is larger than 4, this is more than one whole bar. We can rewrite it as a mixed number: 6/4 = 1 2/4 = 1 1/2. This is not a mistake; it simply means you have collected enough quarter pieces to fill more than one whole. Whenever the top number ends up bigger than the bottom number, change your answer into a mixed number so it is easy to read and understand.
concepts.example: It also helps to say the calculation aloud in plain words. Read 1/5 × 4 as “four lots of one fifth,” and read 1/7 × 3 as “three lots of one seventh.” Saying “lots of” reminds you that multiplying is repeated addition, and it stops you from accidentally changing the denominator. The denominator names the size of each piece, and that size never changes just because you collect more of them.

concepts.title: Dividing a Unit Fraction by a Whole Number
concepts.explanation:
When we divide a unit fraction by a whole number, we are splitting one fraction piece into smaller equal parts. Dividing makes the pieces smaller, which is the opposite of what we did when multiplying.

Here is a real story. Ibrahim has 1/3 of a chocolate bar and wants to share it equally between 2 friends. Each friend gets 1/3 ÷ 2. To see the answer, imagine the whole bar split into three thirds; now cut that one third into two equal pieces. Each little piece is 1/6 of the whole bar, so 1/3 ÷ 2 = 1/6.

Let us picture 1/4 ÷ 2 step by step.

Draw a whole split into 4 parts and shade 1 part. That shaded part is 1/4.

Now split that one shaded part into 2 equal pieces.

Ask: how big is each little piece compared with the whole? The whole is now cut into 8 equal pieces in total, so each little piece is 1/8.

Whole in quarters: [ ■ | _ | _ | _ ] ← this is 1/4. Split the shaded quarter in two → each piece is 1/8 of the whole.

Look carefully at these results and hunt for the pattern:

Do you see it? When you divide 1/n by n, the answer is 1/(n × n). The new denominator is the old one multiplied by itself. That is why 1/5 ÷ 5 = 1/25, because 5 × 5 = 25. More generally, to divide a unit fraction by any whole number you multiply the denominator by that number.

⭐ Quick Rule To divide a unit fraction by a whole number: keep the numerator as 1, and multiply the denominator by the whole number. 1/n ÷ a = 1/(n × a). For example 1/6 ÷ 3 = 1/18, and 1/7 ÷ 5 = 1/35.

Notice how neatly this mirrors multiplying. When you multiply a unit fraction by a whole number, the numerator grows. When you divide a unit fraction by a whole number, the denominator grows and the pieces get smaller. Holding these two ideas side by side will keep you from mixing them up.

Why does the denominator grow when we divide? Think again about the chocolate bar. It was already cut into thirds, so there were 3 equal pieces in the whole. When Ibrahim cuts each of those thirds into 2 smaller pieces, the whole bar is now cut into 3 × 2 = 6 equal pieces, and each little piece is 1/6. The whole never changed size, but it is now split into more pieces, so each piece must be smaller. This is the opposite of sharing sweets between fewer people: the more people who share, the less each one receives.
concepts.example: A helpful check is to ask yourself, “Should my answer be smaller than the fraction I started with?” When you divide a unit fraction by a whole number greater than 1, the answer is always smaller than the fraction you began with. So 1/3 ÷ 2 must be smaller than 1/3, and indeed 1/6 is smaller than 1/3. If you ever divide and get a larger fraction, you know at once that something has gone wrong and it is time to look back at your working.

concepts.title: Multiplying a Decimal by a Whole Number
concepts.explanation:
Multiplying a decimal by a whole number is just like having several copies of that decimal amount. If one book costs 12.50 and Sahra buys 3 books, the total is 12.50 × 3 = 37.50. It is repeated addition again: 12.50 + 12.50 + 12.50.

The key strategy: convert, multiply, convert back

A powerful method is to turn the decimal into a whole number, multiply, then turn it back. Let us calculate 12.9 × 6 carefully.

Estimate first. 10 × 6 = 60 and 20 × 6 = 120, so the answer should be between 60 and 120.

Convert the decimal to a whole number: 12.9 = 129 ÷ 10.

Multiply the whole number: 129 × 6 = 774.

Convert back by dividing by 10: 774 ÷ 10 = 77.4.

Check against the estimate: 77.4 is between 60 and 120, so the answer is sensible.

The estimate is not a waste of time; it is your safety net. If you had made a slip and got 774 as your final answer, the estimate would shout that something is wrong, because 774 is far outside 60 to 120. Estimating first is a habit good mathematicians keep for life.

For simple decimals, a number line makes the idea clear. Take 0.3 × 4, which means four hops of 0.3.

0 ——0.3——0.6——0.9——1.2 (four hops of +0.3)

Starting at 0 we jump 0.3 four times and land on 1.2, so 0.3 × 4 = 1.2.

Another neat method splits the decimal into its whole part and its tenths. Take 1.4 × 5.

Multiply each part: (1 × 5) + (0.4 × 5) = 5 + 2.0.
concepts.example: You can check with the convert-and-convert-back method: 1.4 × 5 = (14 ÷ 10) × 5 = (14 × 5) ÷ 10 = 70 ÷ 10 = 7.0. Two different roads, the same answer, which is exactly what should happen when the maths is correct.

concepts.title: A Problem-Solving Plan
concepts.explanation:
Word problems can feel harder than plain calculations, but only because you must first decide what to calculate. A clear plan removes the worry. Use these six steps every time.

Read the problem carefully, more than once if needed.

Identify what you know and what you need to find.

Choose the right operation: multiply or divide?

Estimate your answer so you know roughly what to expect.

Calculate carefully, showing your working.

Check that your answer makes sense in the story.

The hardest step is usually choosing the operation, so here is a guide. If a story is about collecting several equal amounts (three shirts, four hops, six books), you multiply. If a story is about sharing one amount into equal parts (splitting a chocolate bar between friends), you divide. Reading slowly and picturing the story is the key.

Worked example: “Maryam has 1/6 of a pizza and shares it equally among 3 friends. How much does each friend get?” We know 1/6 of a pizza and 3 friends; we need each share; this is sharing, so we divide: 1/6 ÷ 3 = 1/18. Each friend gets 1/18 of the whole pizza.
concepts.example: Worked example: “A pencil costs 0.75. How much do 4 pencils cost?” We know one price and a quantity; we need the total; this is collecting equal amounts, so we multiply. Estimate: about 0.80 × 4 = 3.20. Calculate: 0.75 × 4 = 3.00. Four pencils cost 3.00, and that is close to our estimate, so it is sensible.

concepts.title: Estimating and Checking
concepts.explanation:
An estimate is a sensible guess made before you calculate. It is never a wild number; it is a thoughtful guess based on rounding to friendly numbers. Estimating protects you from big mistakes, because it tells you the size of answer to expect.

To estimate a decimal multiplication, round the decimal to the nearest whole number and multiply. For 2.1 × 4, round 2.1 to 2, so the estimate is 2 × 4 = 8. When you then calculate the exact answer, 2.1 × 4 = 8.4, you can see it sits just above your estimate of 8, which is exactly right because you rounded 2.1 down a little.

Estimating and calculating work together like two hands: one makes a quick guess, the other does the careful work, and then you compare them. If they are close, you can trust your answer. If they are far apart, stop and look for a slip. Building this habit now will save you from many errors for years to come.

Estimating also helps with fractions, not only decimals. Before working out 1/9 × 12, you might think, “nine ninths make one whole, so twelve ninths must be a little more than one whole.” Sure enough, 12/9 = 1 1/3, which is just over one. And before dividing, you can remind yourself that the answer must be smaller than the fraction you started with. These quick thoughts take only a moment, yet they guard every calculation you make. A wise mathematician once said that the fastest way to be right is to first know roughly what right looks like.

You have now met four operations and two thinking habits. You can multiply a unit fraction by a whole number by growing the numerator. You can divide a unit fraction by a whole number by growing the denominator. You can multiply a decimal by a whole number by converting, multiplying and converting back, or by using place value. And you always estimate first and check that your answer makes sense.

These ideas are not separate islands; they work together. When Amina scales up a recipe for Eid, she multiplies fractions to find how much butter and flour to buy, then multiplies decimals to work out the total cost at the market, and finally divides to share the baking fairly among her cousins. One real task can use every skill in this unit at once. That is why practising them together, out loud and on paper, makes them stick.
concepts.example: The best way to lock these ideas into your memory is to use them with real things around your home. Halve a recipe. Add up the price of several bananas. Share a plate of dates equally and describe the share as a fraction. Every time you do this, your number sense grows stronger, and the harder maths in later units, such as percentages and ratio, will feel far easier. Now let us practise together with some fully worked examples.

methods.title: How to multiply a decimal by a whole number
steps: Estimate by rounding the decimal to a whole number and multiplying.
Convert the decimal to a whole number (for example 1.4 = 14 ÷ 10).
Multiply the whole numbers.
Convert back by dividing by 10 (or 100 for hundredths).
Check your answer against the estimate.

methods.title: How to choose the operation in a word problem
steps: If you are collecting several equal amounts, multiply.
If you are sharing one amount into equal parts, divide.
Estimate the size of the answer before calculating.
Check the answer makes sense in the story.

methods.title: Divide a unit fraction
steps: Solution: Keep the numerator as 1 and multiply the denominator by 5: 7 × 5 = 35.
The pieces got much smaller, which makes sense because we split one seventh into five equal parts.

methods.title: A sharing story
methods.example: Tom has 1/3 of a chocolate bar and divides it equally among 4 people. What fraction of the whole bar does each person get?
steps: Solution: This is sharing, so divide: 1/3 ÷ 4.
Multiply the denominator: 3 × 4 = 12.
Each person gets 1/12 of the whole bar.
A bar model would show one third cut into four thin slices, each a twelfth of the whole.

methods.title: Multiply a decimal, convert-back method
steps: Solution: Estimate first: 2 × 6 = 12, so expect about 12.
Multiply: 18 × 6 = 108.
Convert back: 108 ÷ 10 = 10.8.

methods.title: Multiply a decimal, place value method
steps: Solution: Split 2.3 into 2 + 0.3.
Estimate check: 2 × 5 = 10, and 11.5 is just above 10 because we rounded 2.3 down, so the answer is reasonable.

workedExamples.title: Multiply a unit fraction
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Keep the denominator (eighths) and multiply the numerator: 1 × 6 = 6. So 1/8 × 6 = 6/8, which simplifies to 3/4. Picture a bar in eighths with six parts shaded, and you can see it fills three quarters of the bar.

workedExamples.title: Multiply where the answer passes 1
workedExamples.solution: Solution: 1 × 12 = 12, so the answer is 12/9. Because 12 is bigger than 9, this is more than one whole. Rewrite it: 12/9 = 1 3/9 = 1 1/3. Multiplying a fraction can take you past one whole, and that is perfectly fine.

workedExamples.title: Divide a unit fraction
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Keep the numerator as 1 and multiply the denominator by 5: 7 × 5 = 35. So 1/7 ÷ 5 = 1/35. The pieces got much smaller, which makes sense because we split one seventh into five equal parts.

workedExamples.title: A sharing story
workedExamples.prompt: Tom has 1/3 of a chocolate bar and divides it equally among 4 people. What fraction of the whole bar does each person get?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: This is sharing, so divide: 1/3 ÷ 4. Multiply the denominator: 3 × 4 = 12. Each person gets 1/12 of the whole bar. A bar model would show one third cut into four thin slices, each a twelfth of the whole.

workedExamples.title: Multiply a decimal, convert-back method
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Estimate first: 2 × 6 = 12, so expect about 12. Convert: 1.8 = 18 ÷ 10. Multiply: 18 × 6 = 108. Convert back: 108 ÷ 10 = 10.8. Check: 10.8 is close to the estimate of 12, so it is sensible.

workedExamples.title: Multiply a decimal, place value method
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Split 2.3 into 2 + 0.3. Then (2 × 5) + (0.3 × 5) = 10 + 1.5 = 11.5. Estimate check: 2 × 5 = 10, and 11.5 is just above 10 because we rounded 2.3 down, so the answer is reasonable.

workedExamples.title: A shopping total
workedExamples.prompt: A pencil costs 1.25. How much do 4 pencils cost?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Collecting equal amounts, so multiply: 1.25 × 4. Convert: 1.25 = 125 ÷ 100. Multiply: 125 × 4 = 500. Convert back: 500 ÷ 100 = 5.00. Four pencils cost 5.00. Estimate check: about 1 × 4 = 4 to 1.5 × 4 = 6, and 5.00 sits neatly in between.

workedExamples.title: Choosing the operation
workedExamples.prompt: A recipe needs 1.5 cups of flour. For 3 batches, how much flour is needed in total?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Three equal batches means collecting, so multiply: 1.5 × 3. Split into 1 + 0.5: (1 × 3) + (0.5 × 3) = 3 + 1.5 = 4.5 cups. Estimate check: 2 × 3 = 6 as an upper guess, and 4.5 is a little below, which fits because 1.5 is below 2.

activities.title: Fraction Pizza Party
steps: Draw 4 circles to be pizzas.
Pizza 1: divide into 8 slices, colour 1/8 × 3 slices. Pizza 2: divide into 5 slices, colour 1/5 × 4 slices.
Pizza 3: divide into 6 slices, colour 1/6 × 2 slices. Pizza 4: divide into 4 slices, colour 1/4 × 3 slices.
Under each pizza write the multiplication and its answer.
Challenge: Which pizza has the most coloured slices? If you ate all the coloured slices, how many whole pizzas would that be altogether?

activities.title: Decimal Shopping Spree
activities.materials: paper and pencil (a calculator only for checking).
steps: Price list: pencil 0.75, eraser 1.25, notebook 2.40, ruler 1.80, glue stick 3.50.
For your group buy: 8 pencils, 2 erasers, 5 notebooks, 3 rulers, 2 glue sticks.
Multiply to find the cost of each item type (for example 0.75 × 8 for the pencils).
Add all the costs to find the total for the whole list.
Estimate first each time by rounding, then check your exact answer against the estimate.

activities.title: Fraction Division Detective
steps: Case 1: Draw a chocolate bar in 4 pieces, shade 1/4, then split that piece between 2 friends. What fraction of the whole does each friend get?
Case 2: Draw a metre line, mark 1/3, then cut that third into 3 equal pieces. What fraction of the metre is each piece?
Case 3: Draw a cookie, show 1/6, then divide it among 4 people. What fraction of the whole cookie does each person get?
Detective report: write down the pattern you notice when you divide a unit fraction by a whole number.

activities.title: Mental Math Olympics
activities.materials: a timer and paper for working.
steps: Event 1 (fractions): time yourself on 1/5 × 6, 1/8 × 3, 1/4 × 7, 1/9 × 5, 1/6 × 8. Target: under 2 minutes.
Event 2 (decimals): time yourself on 1.5 × 4, 2.3 × 3, 0.8 × 5, 1.7 × 6, 1.4 × 5. Target: under 3 minutes.
Event 3 (strategy): for 1.8 × 5, 1/4 × 12 and 2.5 × 6, write at least two ways to solve each.
Award yourself a medal: gold for beating both target times, silver for close, bronze for all answers correct.

activities.title: Pattern Discovery Investigation
steps: Fraction pattern: work out 1/2 × 1, 1/2 × 2, 1/2 × 3, 1/2 × 4, 1/2 × 5, 1/2 × 6. What happens with even and odd whole numbers?
Decimal pattern: work out 1.2 × 5, 1.4 × 5, 1.6 × 5, 1.8 × 5, 2.0 × 5. Predict 2.2 × 5 before calculating.

steps: Write two story problems that multiply a unit fraction by a whole number, using sharing food or a craft.

rules.title: Multiplying a Unit Fraction Rule
rules.text: Keep the denominator the same. Multiply the numerator by the whole number. 1/n × a = a/n. Example: 1/5 × 4 = 4/5.

rules.title: Dividing a Unit Fraction Rule
rules.text: Keep the numerator as 1. Multiply the denominator by the whole number. 1/n ÷ a = 1/(n × a). Example: 1/4 ÷ 2 = 1/8.

rules.title: Multiplying a Decimal Rule
rules.text: Estimate first. Convert the decimal to a whole number, multiply, then convert back. Example: 12.9 × 6 = (129 × 6) ÷ 10 = 774 ÷ 10 = 77.4.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Calculate 1/9 × 12 and write it as a mixed number.
Use the pattern to predict 1/6 ÷ 6 without drawing, then explain your reasoning.
Explain two different ways to calculate 2.5 × 4 using mental strategies.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Method 1: 2.5 × 4 = (2 × 4) + (0.5 × 4) = 8 + 2 = 10. Method 2: convert to a whole number: 25 × 4 = 100, then ÷ 10 = 10. Both methods give 10.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Order these from smallest to largest: 1/4 × 2, 1/8 × 3, 1/2 ÷ 2.
Idris says 1/4 × 2 = 1/8. Explain his mistake and give the correct answer.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Idris divided the denominator instead of multiplying the numerator. The denominator (quarters) stays the same when multiplying; only the numerator changes: 1/4 × 2 = 2/4 = 1/2, not 1/8.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Estimating and Checking.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
An estimate is a sensible guess made before you calculate. It is never a wild number; it is a thoughtful guess based on rounding to friendly numbers. Estimating protects you from big mistakes, because it tells you the size of answer to expect.

To estimate a decimal multiplication, round the decimal to the nearest whole number and multiply. For 2.1 × 4, round 2.1 to 2, so the estimate is 2 × 4 = 8. When you then calculate the exact answer, 2.1 × 4 = 8.4, you can see it sits just above your estimate of 8, which is exactly right because you rounded 2.1 down a little.
